In non-pregnant women of reproductive age, Estradiol (E2) is the main Estrogen circulating in the body. Estrogen tends to have a steep rise in the first phase (the follicular phase), and a small rise in the second phase (the luteal phase) of the menstrual cycle. Naturally Estrogen levels decline as your ovarian reserve supply reduces towards perimenopause and menopause.
Due to these natural fluctuations, its essential to monitor Estrogen both throughout the cycle, and from cycle to cycle, to understand what these normal fluctuations are for you.

Knowing your Estrogen levels helps you to understand symptoms associated with low Estrogen, or high Estrogen levels. Forming these associations gives you valuable insights to make lifestyle changes to improve your hormone balance and general wellness.

After ovulation, Progesterone is produced by the cyst that once held the growing egg before it was released. This cyst is known as the corpus luteum and so the release of Progesterone in the second phase of the cycle (the luteal phase) is a key marker that ovulation has occurred, and your cycle is both normal and healthy.
Testing your Progesterone levels not only confirms ovulation, but also indicates any irregularities or issues with your cycle.

Knowing your Progesterone levels helps you to understand symptoms associated with low Progesterone, or high Progesterone levels. Forming these associations gives you valuable insights to make lifestyle changes to improve your hormone balance and general wellness.

Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH) is released by the pituitary gland and plays an important role in the menstrual cycle. At the beginning of the cycle, FSH encourages the follicles in the ovaries to grow and as they do, they release Estrogen. In that way, FSH controls the production of Estrogen, and so is a crucial hormone for the cycle.
Naturally FSH levels rise as you approach perimenopause and menopause, in response to the decline in Estrogen levels.

Testing FSH is important to understand how changes in its levels may be linked to symptoms associated with low FSH, or high FSH levels. Forming these associations gives you valuable insights to make lifestyle changes to improve your hormone balance and general wellness.

Why should I test my hormones?
The only way to know the cause of your imbalance is by testing cyclical hormones

Hormones change daily, between cycles, and throughout our lives, from our first period, through perimenopause, and beyond our reproductive years. This ongoing fluctuation is a normal part of female biology.

Hormones affect the functioning of our entire body. When key hormone levels fall out of balance, this can lead to both mental and physical symptoms, which can be debilitating for many women. During perimenopause in particular, these changes can become more noticeable and harder to interpret without the right tools.

a vital phase in women's health
end of heading, Understanding perimenopause: a vital phase in women's health, level 2

Perimenopause is one of the most significant hormonal transitions in a woman's life, but it continues to be misunderstood. Unlike menopause, which starts after menstruation ends, perimenopause is the overlooked phase leading up to it, bringing symptoms like mood swings, brain fog, irregular periods, sleep changes, and hot flashes. Too many women are dismissed, misdiagnosed, or told to “just deal with it.”

Hormona is changing that. We provide science-backed tools to diagnose and stage perimenopause, along with advanced symptom trackers, expert guidance, and ongoing support. From your first period to your last and beyond, Hormona empowers women to understand their hormones, take control of their health, and feel their best during every stage of life.
heading, Common Questions About At Home Perimenopause Testing, level 3
Who is Hormona Perimenopause test kit for?

Hormona Perimenopause test kit is designed for women experiencing symptoms commonly associated with the menopausal transition — such as mood changes, sleep issues, hot flashes, cycle irregularity, or heavier flow. It combines at-home hormone testing with a specifically designed perimenopause app features to help make sense of these changes.

While perimenopause typically begins in the mid-40s, every woman’s journey is different. Hormona functions as a comprehensive perimenopause tracker and menopause symptom tracker app, making it suitable for anyone who wants to better understand their hormone health during this stage of life — whether you’re already in your 40s, starting to notice changes earlier, or looking for a more tailored alternative to a generic cycle app.

With features that support symptom tracking and HRT tracking, Hormona brings hormone data and cycle insights together in one place. This makes it a strong option for women seeking the best perimenopause app or the best period tracker for perimenopause, designed specifically to support this phase of life. Many women also use it as a perimenopause period tracker to monitor cycle irregularity alongside hormone levels.
What hormones does Hormona Perimenopause test?

Hormona Perimenopause tests three key hormones: FSH (Follicle-Stimulating Hormone), estrogen’s urinary metabolite Estrone-3-Glucuronide (E1G), and progesterone’s urinary metabolite Pregnanediol-Glucuronide (PdG). Together, these hormones provide important insight into the changes that occur during the perimenopausal transition.

The app will let you know which hormone is due for testing, and all you have to do is follow the instructions in the perimenopause app. This means ensuring you’ve got the right test strip, collecting your first-morning urine sample, waiting for the analysis, and then scanning your test to receive your result.

Your test results are stored in the app, allowing you to follow hormone trends over time. As a dedicated perimenopause tracker app, Hormona helps you see how these hormone levels change across cycles, rather than relying on a single measurement.

These hormones naturally shift throughout the perimenopause journey, which can make your cycle feel more unpredictable than usual. FSH rises as the body tries to stimulate the ovaries, estrogen fluctuates significantly before gradually declining, and as ovulation becomes less regular, progesterone levels will vary too before subsiding.

By tracking these hormones together, Hormona functions as a comprehensive perimenopause tracker, helping you better understand what’s happening in your body and why symptoms may change during this stage of life.

What do I get when using the Hormona Perimenopause test kit?

Hormona Perimenopause test kit is designed to help identify the stage you’re at in your perimenopause journey and to support you throughout this phase of life. It combines at-home hormone testing with a specifically designed perimenopause app features to give you clearer, personalised insight.
You’ll get access to a first-of-its-kind solution built with input from real women and

. As a comprehensive perimenopause tracker, the app offers personalized menopause symptom tracking, research-backed relief tips, science-based recipes, and holistic habit-building tools to support you every step of the way.

You’ll also be able to connect with a supportive community, access expert insights, and download a personalised report based on your logged data. By bringing hormone data and symptom tracking together in one place, Hormona provides meaningful support — because your health is worth it.
Does the sample taken have to be first-morning urine?

Research shows that the hormone levels in your first-morning urine has the highest correlation to the previous day’s blood levels. We’ve validated our tests in the lab with this in mind, so testing your first pee of the day will give you the most accurate results.
In which markets will you sell the tests?
Since Hormona is a global brand that aims to help women everywhere, regardless of their location, our tests, just like all our other products, will be available worldwide.
What is the typical perimenopause age range?

The perimenopause age range typically spans the early 40s to mid-50s, though most women notice the first signs in their mid-40s. The average age of perimenopause onset is around 46-47, but this varies significantly from woman to woman. Some experience changes as early as their late 30s, while others don't notice symptoms until their early 50s. Factors like genetics, smoking, and certain medical treatments can influence when perimenopause begins. Because the age range is so wide, tracking your hormone levels over time — rather than waiting for a single diagnosis — is the most reliable way to understand where you are in the transition.
What are the signs that perimenopause is ending?

The clearest signs perimenopause is ending is when your menstrual periods become increasingly far apart and eventually stop altogether. Officially, menopause is confirmed after 12 consecutive months without a period. In the final stages of perimenopause, hot flashes may intensify before gradually subsiding, and you may notice your cycle becoming longer and more irregular rather than shorter. FSH levels, which rise during perimenopause, will remain elevated as you approach menopause. Hormona tracks these hormone shifts over time, helping you understand which stage you're in and what to expect next.
